extracted.intended_audience: middle/high-school students and teachers studying North Carolina state history
extracted.subtask_description: A set of chapter-end comprehension questions for a history textbook covering North Carolina events circa 1790–1827; used to assess student understanding of the narrative and facts presented in each chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling in North Carolina after joining the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the feeling in North Carolina after the State had joined the Union?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Chapter XL discussion of the state's political mood and local sentiment following ratification and admission to the Union; look for references to civic atmosphere and public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of American freedom in Europe
rubrics_metrics.description: How were the effects of American freedom felt in Europe?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Chapter XL paragraphs describing transatlantic influence—how American independence inspired European reformers and affected political thought abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders who disappeared from councils
rubrics_metrics.description: What great leaders disappeared from North Carolina's councils at this time?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify leaders mentioned in the chapter as having left public life or died; use surrounding biography-style passages in Chapter XL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rising influences and governor
rubrics_metrics.description: What then were fast rising to influence? Who became Governor?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check Chapter XL for discussion of emergent political groups or factions and the individual named as becoming governor at that period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and benefit of Raleigh as capital
rubrics_metrics.description: When was Raleigh selected as the capital? Why was locating the capital of great good to the State? Go to the map and point out the city of Raleigh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XL covers the selection of Raleigh and arguments for its location (centrality, accessibility); use the text plus a map to identify Raleigh's position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contests at Assembly meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: What contest would generally arise at meetings of the Assembly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the chapter passage describing recurring political debates in the Assembly—likely contests over representation, policies, or local interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention of religious matters
rubrics_metrics.description: What mention is made of religious matters?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for passages in Chapter XL that address religion's role, revival, denominational activity, or controversies influenced by foreign ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of Christian bodies' usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: How were the Baptists, Presbyterians and other Christian bodies extending their fields of usefulness?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XL notes missionary work, new congregations, social influence and organizational growth—cite those concrete examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor in 1792 and agitating questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Who became Governor in 1792? What is said of him? What questions did Governor Spaight find agitating the people when he came into office?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chapter text naming the governor (Spaight) with the description of his character and the civic issues he confronted (e.g., partisan divisions, foreign affairs influence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Washington and others' consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: How was this matter considered by General Washington and others?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XL recounts Washington's view (non-intervention in foreign affairs) and how leading statesmen counseled restraint—cite that rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of French writers on Americans
rubrics_metrics.description: How were the works of celebrated French writers affecting the people of America?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Chapter XL discussion of Voltaire, Diderot, and the spread of skepticism and fashion influenced by French literature and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion of troubles
rubrics_metrics.description: What was to be the conclusion of all these troubles?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XL posits the eventual outcome (greater liberty, constitutional monarchy, reformed churches); summarize that concluding passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late-eighteenth-century party divisions and Jefferson
rubrics_metrics.description: What was observed towards the latter days of the eighteenth century? Who was one of the political leaders? What views did Mr. Jefferson hold?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI introduces the Federalist/Republican split and Jefferson's advocacy for limited federal powers—cite those characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamilton's leadership and policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Who was the leader of the other great political party? What was Mr. Hamilton's policy?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI names Alexander Hamilton and summarizes his preference for stronger federal authority and skepticism about popular rule—use those details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superior Courts and Judge Spencer's death
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said of the Superior Courts and the Judges? Describe the singular manner of Judge Spencer's death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Chapter XLI's note on court sessions at six villages and the anecdote about Judge Spencer being attacked by a turkey and dying of exhaustion; include court organization details.

rubrics_metrics.name: University seat selection
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said of the University? When was its seat selected, and where?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI explains the 1790 law and the trustees' selection of Chapel Hill as the University site—cite the location on the hillcrest and acreage note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cornerstone laying of East Building
rubrics_metrics.description: When was the cornerstone of the East Building laid? Who officiated? Who delivered the address?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI gives the 1793 date and names Colonel Davie and Rev. Dr. McCorkle—use those particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: University opening and first faculty/student
rubrics_metrics.description: When was the University regularly opened? Who constituted the faculty? Who was the first student to enter? What have been the labors of this institution?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI states the 1795 opening, names Rev. David Kerr and Samuel A. Holmes as faculty and Hinton James as first student—summarize institutional aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land frauds of 1795 and perpetrators
rubrics_metrics.description: What land frauds were perpetrated in 1795? Who were the guilty persons?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI details large tracts improperly located and names James Glasgow, Martin Armstrong, John Armstrong, and Stokeley Donnelson—use text for the fraud description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the land frauds
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the nature of these frauds?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI explains fictitious boundaries, swindling soldiers, states, and the United States—summarize the mechanism described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial of the offenders
rubrics_metrics.description: Give some account of the trial of these offenders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI recounts assembly-ordered courts, 1799 convictions, fines, removal from office, and Judge Haywood's role as defense counsel—cite those outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition of United States affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the condition of affairs throughout the United States at this period?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI discusses partisan conflict, foreign pressures (France), and domestic legislation like the Alien and Sedition Acts—use these contextual points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Alien and Sedition Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the effect of the "Alien and Sedition Laws"?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI summarizes the laws' powers to deport foreigners and indict writers for libel—note public alarm and political usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virginia and Kentucky resolutions and 1800 result
rubrics_metrics.description: What was done by Virginia and Kentucky? What were the resolutions of 1798-99? What party came into power in 1800?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI covers the resolutions asserting state judgment over constitutional infractions and notes the Republican victory in 1800—cite both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commentary on Federalists' decline
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said of the "Federalists"?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLI comments on Federalists' loss of favor and a general observation about the people's wisdom versus learned elites—paraphrase the chapter's editorial note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jefferson's presidency and its character
rubrics_metrics.description: Who was President of the United States at this period? What is said of Jefferson's rule?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII praises Jefferson as political philosopher and party leader, noting consolidation of support—use chapter description.

rubrics_metrics.name: States added and Louisiana purchase
rubrics_metrics.description: What States were added to the Union? What great territory was purchased?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII lists Vermont, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee, and the Louisiana Purchase for $15 million—cite both.

rubrics_metrics.name: British conduct and indignities to Americans
rubrics_metrics.description: How had Great Britain kept the treaty of Paris? What indignities were offered to the American people? How were these things affecting the people?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII outlines British failures to honor the treaty, interference on seas, impressment, and influence on public sentiment leaning toward war—use those examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of education
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said of educational matters?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII notes scarcity of preparatory schools, importance of the University, and general lack of free public education—reference those points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bingham school and other academies
rubrics_metrics.description: What mention is made of the Bingham school? What other schools are mentioned?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII describes Rev. William Bingham's academy (Hillsboro/Mebaneville), Dr. David Caldwell's school, and others—summarize their significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition of free education
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the condition of free education?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII states there were no free schools in the State and only occasional neighborhood efforts—cite the lack of sustained, organized public schooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interests of interior and west populations
rubrics_metrics.description: In what things were the people of the interior and west becoming specially interested?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII discusses demand for conveyance and travel improvements (roads, turnpikes, transport) to reach broader markets—use those examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of turpentine and tar
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said of the production of turpentine and tar?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII notes the long-leaf pine regions produced crude turpentine and tar shipped out for processing elsewhere—summarize local industry details.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Wellborn's 1805 proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: What was proposed by General James Wellborn to the Legislature of 1805?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII reports a proposal to build a state-funded turnpike from Beaufort Harbor to the mountains—cite the measure and its neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coast navigation description
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a general description of coast navigation at this time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII describes hazardous coastal travel, Cape Hatteras dangers, and the limited nature of voyages to NY/Baltimore—use those points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Give some particulars concerning trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII mentions brisk West Indies trade from several towns, exports of staves and provisions, and imports of salt and tropical stores—summarize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of the embargo act
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the embargo act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII describes the embargo forbidding exports to Great Britain and dependencies, paralleling an earlier Continental Congress measure—note enforcement differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: War declared in 1812
rubrics_metrics.description: What war was declared in 1812?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLII cites the War of 1812 declared against Great Britain on June 19, 1812—briefly note causes described (searches, impressment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Governors serving during growth and expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: What Governors had served in North Carolina during the years just considered? Who was Governor at the beginning of the year 1812?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII names James Turner, Nathaniel Alexander, David Stone, Benjamin Smith, and William Hawkins (Governor in 1812)—use chapter listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: US campaign intent and NC troop contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: How had the United States proposed to conduct the campaign? What troops did North Carolina furnish? Who was in command?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII explains the plan to seize Canada, lack of large army, limited NC troop deployment (to Norfolk), and names Major-General Thomas Brown as commander—cite text.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Brown's record and brigade commanders
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said of General Brown's past record? Who were his brigade commanders?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII notes Brown's Revolutionary service and lists brigade commanders Thomas Davis and James F. Dickinson—use those mentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military preparations in North Carolina
rubrics_metrics.description: What military preparations were made in North Carolina?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII details camps, levies at Wadesboro, garrisons at Wilmington and Beaufort, and commanders Maurice Moore and John Roberts—summarize these defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: NC officers under Winfield Scott
rubrics_metrics.description: What two North Carolina officers were winning distinction under General Winfield Scott? In what branch of the army were they serving?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII names William Gibbs McNeill and William McRee as colonels in the corps of engineers—cite their significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affairs on the seas and naval officer
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said of affairs on the seas? What North Carolina naval officer was distinguishing himself?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII discusses British naval superiority and notable NC naval officer Johnston Blakeley—use text about sea actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of Blakeley's exploits and captures
rubrics_metrics.description: Give an account of some of his bold and heroic exploits. How many English vessels did he capture?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII recounts Blakeley's capture of the Reindeer, later captures including fifteen merchant vessels, burning prizes, and refitting—use those specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: What became known after Blakeley
rubrics_metrics.description: What is known of him after this?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII notes that Blakeley perished at sea under unknown circumstances; his reputation endured—cite this concluding note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Otway Burns and commemoration
rubrics_metrics.description: What other seaman was distinguishing himself for his bravery? How is his name commemorated in the State?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII names Captain Otway Burns of the Snap-Dragon and notes Burnsville was named in his honor—use those items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force sent against the Indians and commander
rubrics_metrics.description: Who was sent against the Indians? What great general was in command of all this force?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII describes a North Carolina regiment under Colonel Joseph Graham and General Andrew Jackson commanding the larger force—cite the Creek conflict context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success of Jackson's expedition
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the success of General Jackson's expedition?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII summarizes Jackson's swift victory, the death of Weathersford's warriors, and the condition that led to Weathersford's surrender—use that narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of the War of 1812
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said of the end of the war of 1812?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIII explains the 1815 peace that ended hostilities without resolving the war's causes and notes treaty ratification on February 7, 1815—include impotent lingering issues like impressment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition of NC after the War of 1812
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the condition of North Carolina after the war of 1812?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV describes renewed trade, scarcity of imported goods easing, and general economic relief—use opening paragraphs of the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of counties and legislative representation
rubrics_metrics.description: How many counties were in North Carolina in 1815? What is said of the representation in the General Assembly? What towns had special privileges?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV states the State had sixty-two counties, each sending one Senator and two House members, and lists borough towns like Edenton, New Bern, Wilmington, etc., with extra representation—cite these facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth of the Moravian settlement at Salem
rubrics_metrics.description: Give some account of the growth of the Moravian settlement at Salem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV discusses Wachovia's thrift, the founding of a female seminary in 1804, and Salem's role as an educational center—use those details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of towns and villages
rubrics_metrics.description: Give some description of various towns and villages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV contrasts Raleigh (~800 people), Fayetteville, Wilmington, New Bern, and notes changes in relative importance among towns—summarize population/trade notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dr. Joseph Caldwell's efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: What efforts was Dr. Joseph Caldwell putting forth for the advancement of the State?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV credits Caldwell's presidency of the University, his advocacy for education and internal improvements, and an 1827 address on railways—cite his influence and initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth among Methodist churches
rubrics_metrics.description: What growth was seen among the Methodist churches?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV notes increasing Methodist conferences, churches, and itinerant preachers—use that expansion narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head of the Episcopal Church and Bishop Ravenscroft
rubrics_metrics.description: Who was at the head of the Episcopal Church? What is said of Bishop Ravenscroft?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV names John Stark Ravenscroft as bishop (consecrated 1816) and describes his piety and character—include the chapter's appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eminent Presbyterian divines and their benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Who were the most eminent Presbyterian divines? What benefit was derived from their labors?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV lists Drs. McCorkle, Caldwell, and Hall and credits them with refuting French atheism and contributing learning and devotion—summarize their roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political leaders named
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention the political leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV highlights William Gaston, Bartlett Yancey, James Iredell (another), John Stanly, George E. Badger, Romulus M. Saunders—use chapter references to their reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of the Supreme Court and Justices
rubrics_metrics.description: Through whose efforts was the Supreme Court established? Who were the Justices?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV credits Bartlett Yancey and names John Louis Taylor (Chief-Justice), Leonard Henderson, and John Hall as associates—cite establishment and roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Era of "Good Feeling"
rubrics_metrics.description: What was this period called?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV refers to the period as the era of 'Good Feeling'—note the chapter's contextualization with growing sectional tensions over slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question agitating the people
rubrics_metrics.description: What question was greatly agitating the people?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLIV points to the slavery question in the Territories and the Missouri Compromise as the contentious issue—use the chapter discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic stagnation despite national growth
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said about North Carolina's material growth and emigration?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLV (opening) notes that while the nation grew, NC experienced emigration of population and wealth to the South and West, limiting local prosperity—cite these observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immigration comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said of immigration to North Carolina versus other regions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLV observes little immigration into NC during the prior century compared with Northern/Western states and declining settler streams—use the chapter's demographic note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-1800 party alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: After the overthrow of the Federalists by Mr. Jefferson, what was the national party situation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLV explains the dominance of Democratic-Republicans and continuing adherents to Hamiltonian views; summarize the absence of old Federalist contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the Democratic-Republican era
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Mr. Madison and his successors what was the party situation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLV states there was effectively one party (Democratic-Republicans), and political advancement required professing its faith—use this political context.

rubrics_metrics.name: La Fayette's 1825 visit
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said of General La Fayette's visit in 1825?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLV recounts Lafayette's celebrated tour, national reception, and return aboard the Brandywine—note public veneration and congressional honors.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1825 cotton price surge
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said of the extraordinary advance in the price of cotton in 1825?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLV mentions a rise from twelve to thirty-two cents, its temporary nature, and financial ruin for some—summarize as a market bubble example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election of John Quincy Adams and party split
rubrics_metrics.description: What resulted from the election of John Quincy Adams in 1825? How did it affect party lines?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLV explains Adams' contested election, Jackson's leadership of Democrats, and the emergence of Whigs opposing Jackson—use the chapter's party realignment notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whig vs Democrat policy differences
rubrics_metrics.description: What policies did the Whigs advocate and how did Democrats differ under Jackson?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLV summarizes Whig support for the Bank, protective tariffs, and distribution of public land funds; Jacksonian Democrats favored tariff for revenue and opposed the Bank—cite those contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan rancor and social effects
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said about rancor between Whigs and Democrats?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter XLV comments on growing social animosity (duels, broken amenities) despite shared citizenship and the chapter's moral rebuke—use those observations.
